None of those declarations exist for a Windows target, and `zio.ev.NetRecv.init` takes `Backend.NetHandle`, which on the iocp backend is a socket handle and not `std.c.fd_t`. build.zig registers the example unconditionally in the `examples` list, and `.github/workflows/test.yml` runs `check.sh --full` on `windows-latest`, which runs `zig build examples`. The Windows CI job therefore fails to compile. No other example in `examples/` touches `std.c` at all; zio already offers portable primitives for this (`zio.net`, `zio.PipePair`). Guard the example by target, or build it from the portable API."}, {"file": "examples/cq_spurious_select_repro.zig", "line": 96, "severity": "major", "category": "stability", "title": "`driver` unwinds with completions still armed on its own coroutine stack", "body": "`cq`, `recv_op`, `recv_buf`, `iov` and `t1` all live in the generation's stack frame, and the function has no `defer cq.cancelAll(...)` (every CompletionQueue example and test in src/completion_queue.zig has one). Every early exit leaves one or both operations pending in the event loop: `return error.Spurious` at line 96, `return err` at line 98, a canceled `try zio.select` at line 86, and a failing `try cq.submit`. The task then returns, and src/task.zig:483 releases the coroutine stack back to the stack pool. When the still-armed recv or timer later fires, the backend writes its result into the recycled `NetRecv` bytes and `ownerCallback` locks the mutex of a `CompletionQueue` that no longer exists, pushing onto its list and calling `Futex.wake` on that address. The deferred `std.c.close(fds[0])` at line 68 also runs while the recv is armed on that descriptor. The consequence is memory corruption of whatever task next takes that stack, and it fires on exactly the path the reproducer exists to reach, so a detected reproduction is followed by an unrelated crash or a false result in another worker."}, {"file": "examples/cq_spurious_select_repro.zig", "line": 49, "severity": "major", "category": "correctness", "title": "The flooder can write to a descriptor the driver has already closed", "body": "The flooder loads `sh.feed_fd` and then calls `std.c.write(fd, ...)`. The driver runs on another executor thread and, at the end of a generation, stores -1 and closes `fds[1]` (lines 73 and 69). Nothing orders the flooder's load against those two steps: the flooder can read a valid descriptor, be descheduled by the OS, and issue the write after the close. The run churns two descriptors per generation for up to 20000 generations across 8 workers, so the closed number is reused almost immediately, usually by another worker's socketpair but potentially by any descriptor the process opens. The write then lands in an unrelated file or socket. For a tool whose only job is to produce trustworthy evidence, that is a silent corruption of the experiment as well as a descriptor use-after-close. Hand the write end to the flooder for the whole run, or guard the descriptor's lifetime with a lock or a reference count."}, {"file": "examples/cq_spurious_select_repro.zig", "line": 175, "severity": "minor", "category": "correctness", "title": "A reproduction does not stop the other drivers, so exit 2 arrives long after the SPURIOUS line", "body": "`Shared.stop` is only read by `flooder`; `driver` never checks it, and nothing else tells the remaining drivers to give up. When one driver detects the bug and returns `error.Spurious`, the other 7 keep running their full budget of 20000 generations x 64 selects, and the join loop in `go` walks the handles in index order, so `std.process.exit(2)` waits for the slowest of them. Each generation costs at least the 50 us timer plus a socketpair setup, so the wait is minutes, not the \"~1 s\" the file header describes. The header states the reproducer \"detects the spurious win itself: a SPURIOUS line and exit 2\"; only the print is prompt. Set a shared stop flag from the detecting driver and have `driver` check it in the generation loop."}, {"file": "examples/cq_spurious_select_repro.zig", "line": 186, "severity": "minor", "category": "tests", "title": "The clean report counts the requested budget, not the work the probe actually did", "body": "On the no-reproduction path the tool prints only `n_workers`, `gens` and `spg`, which are the arguments it was given. It never counts how many times the `.io` arm won a select, how many completions `next()` handed out, or how many times the recv completed. A run where the window is never opened prints exactly the same line as a run that exercised it hard: for example, if the channel arm wins every select the queue arm is never claimed, or if the recv never completes only the timer drives the queue. Exit 0 then reads as \"the bug is gone\" when it may mean \"the instrument never fired\". Count the io-arm wins and the completions consumed, print them with the clean line, and exit non-zero when either is zero."}, {"file": "examples/cq_spurious_select_repro.zig", "line": 169, "severity": "minor", "category": "stability", "title": "A failed spawn leaves running tasks pointing at freed memory", "body": "The spawn loop in `go` has no `errdefer`. If `runtime.spawn` fails part way through, `go` returns the error and its deferred `alloc.free` calls release `shs`, `chans` and `bufs` while the flooders and drivers already spawned keep running against those buffers, and against `spurious`, which lives in `go`'s own coroutine frame. The already-created `JoinHandle`s are also dropped without a join or a cancel, so their awaitables are never released. Cancel and join the handles spawned so far with an `errdefer` before the frees."}]}
